intro:
Al-Fātiḥah is the sūrah that opens the Book and the sūrah that opens a Muslim's day. It has seven verses, and its names tell the story of its work. Al-Baghawī lists three that are well known. It is called the Opener of the Book because the Qur'an begins with it, the Mother of the Qur'an and the Mother of the Book because it is the root the rest of the Book grows out of. It is called the Seven Repeated Verses because its seven lines are read again and again in every prayer. He notes that the scholars agree on the count of seven, and that the name which is repeated comes from the fact that the sūrah is recited in every unit of prayer.

Ibn Kathīr collects the reports that carry the same names. He says the sūrah was revealed in Makkah, at the start of the mission, when the first Muslims had almost nothing to read and no mosque to read it in. That setting matters for the sūrah's tone. A small community is taught a prayer that begins with praise and ends with a request for guidance, which is the shape of the whole religion. It asks for no victory, no wealth and no long life. It asks to be shown the road and kept on it.

The sūrah is also a conversation. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim carries the report of Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said God has divided the prayer into two halves, one for Him and one for His servant. When the servant says that all praise belongs to God, the Lord of all worlds, God answers that His servant has praised Him. When the servant reaches the middle of the sūrah and says that he worships God alone and asks His help alone, God answers that the verse is shared between them. When the servant asks for guidance, God answers that the guidance is his, and he will have what he asks for. The prayer is therefore a dialogue, and the reader is never speaking into an empty room.

The order of the sūrah is worth noticing before the verses are read one at a time. It begins with a name, then with praise, then with the two names of mercy, then with the day of account, and only then does it ask for anything. This is not a formality. A reader who has praised God for the worlds He raised is in a different position when he asks to be guided, because he already knows who is speaking and who is listening. The praise is a doorway, and the request walks through it.

The ten works used for this chapter read the sūrah from different angles. Al-Ṭabarī tracks the reports back to the Companions and the Successors and refuses to invent meaning. Al-Qurṭubī gathers the rulings that grow out of the words, down to whether the opening line belongs to the sūrah at all. Al-Baghawī keeps the narrative short and clear. Ibn Kathīr tells the stories in full. Al-Alūsī digs into the language and the grammar. Al-Jalālayn gives the plain running sense, Ibn ʿAbbās the earliest gloss. Al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿUthaymīn and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explain what the words mean for someone living now. Read together, they make the sūrah walk off the page and into a week.

verses.1:
> In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**THE WORDS THAT OPEN EVERY GOOD WORK**

The sūrah begins with ***“In the Name of Allah”***, and the line was not chosen by the community. Al-Ṭabarī reads the words as the education of a prophet. God taught His messenger to place His names before everything he did, and then made that habit a path for the rest of creation, so that a meal, a journey and a letter all begin the same way. In his reading the little word at the front carries a whole sentence that is left unsaid: the speaker is saying that he starts this act with the name of God. The name is doing the work of a declaration.

The wording itself was taught in stages. Al-Alūsī reports that the Prophet ﷺ first used a shorter form of the line, and al-Qurṭubī cites the report from Abū Dāwūd's collection, that the messenger wrote the name of God alone. The final wording is the one Noah spoke as the ark was loaded: (11:41 — **“In the Name of Allah it will sail and cast anchor. Surely my Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**). The two names of mercy came next, and the last step is also recorded in the Book, in the letter of Solomon that the Qur'an preserves: (27:30 — **“It is from Solomon, and it reads: ‘In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”**). Al-Qurṭubī adds that the phrase is a pledge spoken by God over every sūrah, a word of assurance that what follows is true and that He will keep what He has promised in it.

Al-Qurṭubī also notes the disagreement among the early scholars about the legal status of the line. Mālik held that it is not counted as a verse of any sūrah, Ibn al-Mubārak held that it opens every sūrah as a verse. Al-Shāfiʿī held that it is a verse of this sūrah, with two views about the others. All of them agree that it stands in the Qur'an in the sūrah of the ant, and every one of them recites it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reports that Abū Ḥanīfah read it quietly before the sūrah rather than as a counted verse of it, and that the community has never stopped using it either way.

The practical weight of the line shows in how much of a life it covers. A person says it before eating, before travelling, before a difficult conversation. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the name as the beginning of blessing in any work, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn teaches it as the confession that no act of a servant stands on its own strength. A craftsman who walks into a workshop that is not his own and picks up another man's tools says the owner's name first. That is how the sentence works: the day's work is named after its owner before it begins.

**THREE NAMES IN ONE LINE**

The second half of the verse gives God two titles from a single root: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***. Al-Ṭabarī explains the name Allāh as the name of the One who is worshipped, the One whose existence no one shares and whose right to devotion nothing else can touch. Al-Qurṭubī draws the difference between the two titles that follow. The Most Compassionate is a name of mercy that reaches every creature in this world, whether or not a person ever thanks Him for it, while the Most Merciful is the mercy kept for the people who believe. The first fills the sky with rain on a field and on a rock; the second turns the rain into a harvest for the people who take the road.

The Book uses both titles for the same God and never as rivals: (7:156 — **“My mercy encompasses everything. I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations”**). Al-Qurṭubī also records that the Most Compassionate is a name God kept for Himself, so that no idol and no rival was ever called by it, and Ibn Kathīr reports the same point from the earliest scholars. Al-Saʿdī adds a grammatical key that opens the whole line: the word for name stands alone and is joined to God, so the servant who begins with that word is not naming one title out of many. He reaches for every beautiful name at once. The two titles of mercy are then given as the ones a person needs before anything else.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads mercy as the gift that preceded the command, and al-Jalālayn gives the plain sense of the pair in a single move: the One who shows mercy widely, and the One who shows it especially. The difference is not a small piece of grammar. A religion whose first sentence names power and then stops becomes a religion of fear. This sūrah names mercy before it mentions the final day, and it puts the day in the middle of the mercy rather than before it.

Al-Alūsī gathers the readings under the same conclusion, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn draws the lesson for practice: the servant begins his work under a name that promises kindness, so he should not begin it in despair. Imagine a man who goes to the house of a judge with a heavy case hanging over him. He reaches the gate and finds that the door carries the name of the kindest man in the city, written in the owner's own hand. He reads the name before he knocks, and the reading changes how he knocks.

**WHAT A READER DOES WITH THE LINE**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes that the sūrah does not open with a command, a warning or a rule. It opens with a name, which means the first thing the Book asks of a reader is attention to who is speaking to him. Ibn Kathīr records the report, graded sound by al-Tirmidhī, that this sūrah is the Mother of the Book and the seven repeated verses. If a reader holds that description in mind, the line at the head of it is the title page of a document that will be read in every prayer until the end of a life.

Al-Saʿdī notes that the mercy named here is not a mood but an act, because the provision of the servant and his guidance both flow from it. That gives the opening line a claim on the day. A person who says it and then treats his household with harshness has spoken a sentence he has not used. A person who says it before a bill, a court or a hospital visit has put the day's outcome in the hand he named.

The scholars of the community also kept the line connected to the prayer. Al-Qurṭubī reports the schools on where it is recited aloud, and every school keeps it in the prayer in some form. Ibn Kathīr mentions the report of the Prophet ﷺ and his two companions beginning the recitation with the praise of God, which Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī carries. The habits differ; the line does not disappear.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that the one who says these words is placing his whole affair under the name of the One who owns it. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught the same truth to students who asked how a person should begin a new job, a journey or a marriage. The answer was never a formula to say and forget. It was a sentence to mean, and meaning it takes a moment. That moment is the first thing this sūrah teaches, and it is the reason the Book opens the way it does.
verses.2:
> All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds

**THE SENTENCE THAT NAMES THE GIVER**

The second verse gathers all praise under one owner: ***“All praise is for Allah”***. Al-Ṭabarī reads praise here as thankfulness joined to humility, an acknowledgment that the gift and the guidance came first and the servant only received them. He records the report from Ibn ʿAbbās that the angel Gabriel told the Prophet ﷺ to say the sentence, and he also records his own judgement that the chain carrying that report is not strong. Al-Jalālayn notes that the definite article in the Arabic does its work: praise, all of it that any creature could offer, belongs to God and to no one beside Him.

Al-Saʿdī opens the sentence further. Praise, he says, is spoken of God for two things at once: for His attributes, which are perfect, and for His acts, which move between generosity and justice. Nothing in the sky or in a person's week falls outside the two, so the praise covers what a person understands and what he does not. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same sentence as the praise of a creature for the kindness of its Maker. The Book repeats the sentence at the head of five sūrahs and in the middle of others: (6:1 — **“All praise is for Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light. Yet the disbelievers set up equals to their Lord”**).

The word order is a lesson in manners. Praise comes before the request, and the praise is stated as a fact rather than offered as a bargain. Al-Baghawī notes that the sentence is the opening of speech rather than the end of it, and that everything the sūrah asks for afterwards stands on it. A servant who has said that all praise belongs to God has already admitted that whatever he is about to ask for is a gift rather than a wage.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the practical conclusion: the sentence is the answer to a heart that measures God by the last thing that went wrong. Ibn ʿUthaymīn teaches that the believer's praise is not a payment for favours already received but the recognition of a standing fact, true in a hard year as much as in an easy one. Imagine a man who keeps a ledger of every kindness a neighbour has shown him, and who reads the first page of it aloud before he asks for anything. The reading is not flattery, and it is the reason the request can be made at all.

**THE LORD WHO RAISES EVERYTHING**

The verse then says who the praised One is: ***“Lord of all worlds”***. Al-Baghawī explains that the word for Lord carries the sense of one who owns, repairs and raises, and that the plural covers every kind of being that exists. He lists them: the heavens and the earth, the angels, the jinn, human beings, animals, plants, and everything in between. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the same sense in plain English: to nurture is to bring a thing along by stages until it reaches its proper end. No created thing can do that for itself, which is why the title belongs to God alone.

Al-Saʿdī divides that care into two. The care that every creature shares is creation, provision and the guidance to what keeps it alive; the special care is kept for the people who believe. It works by faith, by help at the right moment and by protection from what would ruin them. He notes that the prophets asked for almost everything by this title, because every request they had was a request for care they could not supply themselves. Al-Qurṭubī records the scholars' reading that the worlds are gathered by kind rather than by place, so a farmer, a star and an ant are each a world tended by the same hand.

The Book teaches the title with stories rather than definitions. Pharaoh asked about it, and Moses answered with the sky and the ground: (26:23 — **“And what is ‘the Lord of all worlds’?””**), then (26:24 — **“the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith”**). Abraham used the title when he surrendered: (2:131 — **“I submit to the Lord of all worlds”**). The Book closes the same claim over the whole creation: (7:54 — **“Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds”**). Ibn Kathīr points out that this is why the sentence is so large: it does not say that God made the world once and stepped away; it says He is raising it now.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn draws the lesson for a reader who feels small. If the One being praised is the Lord of every world, then no world of the reader is outside the care being named, not his work, not his marriage, not his health. Al-Alūsī notes that the title also carries a duty: a servant who admits that he is being raised should expect the raising to include correction, because a farmer who tends a tree cuts it as well as waters it.

**WHAT THE PRAYER IS ANSWERED WITH**

Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim carries the report of Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said God has divided the prayer into two halves, and that when a servant says the words of this verse, God answers that His servant has praised Him. Al-Baghawī quotes the same report in full, verse by verse, so that the whole sūrah is shown as a conversation: praise is answered with praise, and the request at the end is answered with a promise of guidance. Al-Qurṭubī adds that the answer is not spoken aloud for the worshipper to hear, and that the servant's part is to say the words with attention as though the reply were arriving.

Hadith and grammar meet here in a way that changes the reading. Ibn Kathīr reports that the sūrah is called the seven repeated verses because it is recited in every unit of prayer, and the division report explains what those repetitions are for. Al-Jalālayn observes that the sūrah moves from speaking about God to speaking to Him, and this verse is the hinge. Al-Saʿdī notes that the word for Lord stands beside the word for worlds so that the servant's praise covers provision and guidance in one thought.

A reader can hold the two halves of this verse in a single habit. When food arrives, the first sentence names the One who sent it. When a difficulty arrives, the same sentence marks the One who is managing the difficulty. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that one who knows God by this title does not complain about the way the world is run. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught students that praise in a hard season is the difference between a servant and a guest who rates the food.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān closes the discussion with a boundary that keeps the verse honest: praise of God is not the same as praise of the world. The next verse names mercy, the verse after it names the day of accounting, and the reader is carried through the whole picture before he is allowed to ask for anything. That order is the sūrah's own protection against a religion of comfort. The praise comes first, the mercy comes first, and the accounting is named before the request is made.
verses.3:
> the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**WHY MERCY IS NAMED AFTER LORDSHIP**

The verse repeats the two titles from the opening line and gives them a place of their own: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***. Al-Qurṭubī reads the placement as care for the listener. The title Lord of all worlds carries a warning, because a Lord owns, commands and corrects. The two names of mercy are set beside it so that fear and hope travel together, and the servant obeys with both hands rather than with one. He compares the arrangement to the verse that gathers the same pair: (15:49 — **“I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**), followed immediately by (15:50 — **“that My torment is indeed the most painful”**).

Al-Ṭabarī pauses over the repetition itself, because the words stand here and in the line that opens the sūrah. He argues from it that the opening line is not counted as a verse of this sūrah, since the Book never places two identical verses side by side without speech between them. Al-Qurṭubī reports the opposite position of al-Shāfiʿī, and the disagreement is an old one among scholars who agreed on everything a reader depends on. Al-Alūsī records that most of them held the sūrah to be Makkan and among the earliest of what was revealed, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the mention of mercy in this place as a reminder that God did not take up the care of the universe out of any compulsion or need, since the creation adds nothing to Him.

The point Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws is worth holding onto. God did not take up the care of the creation because anything forced Him to it, and the universe adds nothing to Him. He raises what He made out of His own mercy, and the verse names that mercy in the middle of a prayer so that the servant knows the ground he is standing on. Al-Saʿdī writes that every blessing a person can name, from the air he breathes to the faith in his chest, is a trace of this one quality, and the mercy reaches every living thing before it settles in full on the people who follow God's messengers.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the pair as the Gentle and the Kind, and al-Jalālayn defines the word behind them as the will to do good for the one who is owed it. Ibn Kathīr keeps the two titles at the centre of the sūrah and repeats al-Qurṭubī's comparison between warning and encouragement. A reader who has been frightened by the size of the Lord of the worlds is handed a sentence that keeps him from running away. A reader who has grown careless about that Lord is handed the same sentence to keep him from presuming on it.

**TWO NAMES FROM ONE ROOT**

The two titles share a root, and the difference between them is a difference of reach. Al-Qurṭubī explains that the first name describes mercy poured out without limit in this life, on the just and the unjust, on the believer and the one who denies Him, in the rain and in the harvest and in the breath. The second describes the mercy that is kept for the people who turn to Him, and it is the mercy that saves on the day the sūrah names next. Al-Saʿdī puts the same reading in two sentences: the wide mercy reaches everything that lives, and the settled mercy is written for those who avoid evil, give in charity and believe in what their Lord sent down.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that both Arabic words are built to carry greatness, so a reader is not listening to two small compliments but to a claim about the scale of the kindness that holds him up. Al-Alūsī collects the reports that no creature was ever named with the first of the two, and Ibn Kathīr repeats the point from the earliest scholars. The Book itself asks the reader to look for the two names in creation, and it states the wideness of the first with a plain sentence: (6:12 — **“He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment”**).

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that the servant who understands the two names neither despairs in a hard year nor grows proud in an easy one. The mercy that gives him the year is the mercy that will ask him about it. Al-Jalālayn adds that the second title carries the sense of a mercy that actually arrives, not a wish that stays in the air. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught the same thing to students in a sentence worth writing on a wall: the mercy of God is not a weakness that overlooks everything, and it is not a severity that enjoys punishing.

Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim carries the report of Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said that if the believer knew the punishment that is with God, not one of them would hope for His garden, and that if the one who denies Him knew the mercy that is with God, not one of them would despair of it. Al-Qurṭubī quotes the same report in his reading of this verse, and Ibn Kathīr quotes it too, which is an unusual sign of agreement between two very different books. The verse stops a person at the point where he might take either of the two names and forget the other.

**WHAT THE TWO NAMES ASK OF A READER**

Al-Baghawī quotes the report that the Prophet ﷺ described the sūrah as a conversation between a servant and his Lord, and that in this verse the servant's words are answered with the reply that he has praised God with both names. That reply is a claim on the reader's day. A person who asks God to be merciful to him and then refuses mercy to a servant, a debtor or a child has spoken a sentence that he does not mean. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have made the same point in a short tradition: the one who shows mercy will find it.

Al-Saʿdī counts the test of the two names in a household. The mercy named here does not wait for people to be good before it works, since the sun rises on a village that never thanks its Maker. A parent who keeps that picture in front of him can keep feeding a difficult child. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that the servant should imitate the reach of the mercy and not only its warmth, so that his kindness lands on people who cannot repay him. That is why the sūrah puts these two names before the day of account rather than after it: the reckoning will be measured by a hand that has already been generous.

The image the scholars keep returning to is a field and its rain. The wide mercy is the rain that falls on every plot, on the one whose owner planted it and on the one that lies empty. The settled mercy is the crop that comes up where the seed was put. A farmer who has watched a dry field turn green does not need a lecture on the first; a farmer who has ever harvested anything understands the second. The verse puts both kinds of water in the same line and asks the reader which field he is.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān closes the discussion with the note that the sūrah mentions mercy before it mentions the day of judgment, so that a reader comes to the account already knowing the character of the accountant. Al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence short: the One described here wants what is good for those who turn to Him. A person can build an entire week on that sentence, and the sūrah expects him to.
verses.4:
> Master of the Day of Judgment

**THE DAY THAT SETTLES EVERY CLAIM**

The sūrah then names the day that gives the mercy its weight: ***“Master of the Day of Judgment”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the word din as the day of repayment, the day the dead are raised and every account is brought to a close. Ibn ʿAbbās calls the Master of that day the judge who settles what the creation disputed, and there is no judge beside Him. Al-Qurṭubī reports the same sense from the scholars of the language, that the word carries both repayment and the authority that repays.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān asks the question a careful reader would ask. God owns everything today and tomorrow, so why is this one day singled out? Its answer is that the day of account is when the ownership becomes impossible to dispute. A tyrant can pretend to rule for a lifetime, and a wealthy man can buy influence for decades, and both of them will stop pretending when the record is opened. The Book pictures the moment in a single question: (40:16 — **“Who does all authority belong to this Day? To Allah—the One, the Supreme”**). Al-Jalālayn cites the same verse for the same reason.

The Book leaves no room to argue with the day. It says that no soul will be of any benefit to another on it, and that all authority belongs to God: (82:19 — **“the Day no soul will be of ˹any˺ benefit to another whatsoever, for all authority on that Day belongs to Allah ˹entirely˺”**). It also tells the reader that the hour is hidden on purpose, and that effort, not timing, is what a person is asked about: (20:15 — **“My Will is to keep it hidden, so that every soul may be rewarded according to their efforts”**). Al-Qurṭubī notes that the day is called by many names in the Book, and that each name presents a different face of the same appointment. A reader who has seen a court adjourn for years and then watched every party stand when the judge finally enters understands the image the sūrah is using.

Al-Saʿdī makes the connection to the previous verse in one move. Mercy has just been named, and the day of account is named straight after it, which tells the reader that the mercy and the reckoning come from one Lord and are not in competition. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that a person who believes in the day of account will treat his small wrongs as real, because the court that will hear them never sleeps. Al-Baghawī notes that the sūrah was called the Seven Repeated Verses because this line, like the others, returns in every unit of every prayer, so the community repeats its belief in the accounting dozens of times a day.

**TWO READINGS, ONE CLAIM**

The Arabic word in this verse can be read in two ways, and both are old. Al-Ṭabarī lists the reciters who read it one way and those who read it the other, and he asks what each reading carries. The reading that gives the sense of king describes the day when kingship belongs to God alone, with no tyrant left to contest it. The reading that gives the sense of owner describes the day when possession is total and undivided. He notes that the two meanings end in the same place, because the day of account is the day that every claim of ownership is finally measured.

Al-Qurṭubī gathers four dialect forms of the word and then reports the debate among the scholars about which is stronger. The case for the reading of kingship rests on the fact that every king owns something, while not every owner is a king, and that the command of a king runs through the property of every owner under him. The case for the reading of ownership rests on the fact that possession is the wider claim and the one that no one can return to another man. He states that both readings are reported from the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and that al-Tirmidhī recorded them.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the difference does not divide the community. The sentence is not a description of one quality among many; it is a statement of who is in charge of the appointment every person must keep. Al-Jalālayn reads the word in the sense of master of the whole affair on that day, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as the arbitrator whose ruling is final. A reader who has heard two spellings of the same road sign has not been given two roads. The sūrah places the word after the two names of mercy so that the traveller knows both the destination and the driver.

Al-Alūsī notes that the Book describes God by these royal names in many sūrahs, and that the names carry obligation as much as comfort. A servant who says that God owns the day of account has admitted that his account is being kept by someone with the authority to settle it. That admission is the reason the sūrah can move on to worship in the next verse without a break. Praise has been given, mercy has been named, the accounting has been acknowledged, and only then does the servant speak about himself.

**WHERE THE KINGS WILL BE STANDING**

Ibn Kathīr reports two traditions from the two most trusted collections on this title. The first is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, that the most shameful name before God is carried by a man who calls himself the king of kings, since no owner exists besides God. The second is in the same two collections: on the day of judgment God will fold the heavens in His right hand and ask where the kings of the earth are, where the tyrants are, where the proud are. The question is not answered in the report, and the silence is the answer.

Al-Qurṭubī draws the point the sūrah is making for the reader's own week. A person who has spent his energy building a small kingdom at home or at work has been told in advance where those kingdoms will be standing. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a statement about a courtroom with a single judge. Al-Saʿdī reads it as a statement about a debt that is being recorded in full. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that the believer keeps the two names of mercy in one hand and this title in the other, because hope without fear becomes carelessness, and fear without hope becomes despair.

The Book repeats the announcement of that day in a way a reader can see. It describes people who asked when the day would come: (51:12 — **“When is this Day of Judgment”**). It answers the mockery in the next stage of the story: (56:56 — **“This will be their accommodation on the Day of Judgment”**). Al-Jalālayn notes that the day is named here in a sūrah of mercy so that a careless person hears it in time, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the two traditions of the day's title at the centre of his reading.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān closes with the observation that the sūrah mentions a king and a day together so that the reader measures his own plans against both. A farmer's account is settled on a date he does not choose, by an owner who supplied the seed, the soil and the rain. The sūrah has just said the same thing about mercy, and this verse adds the date. The next line is the moment the servant finally opens his mouth and speaks about his own part in the transaction.
verses.5:
> You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help

**THE MOMENT THE SERVANT TURNS AND SPEAKS**

For four lines the sūrah has been speaking about God, and then the words change direction: ***“You ˹alone˺ we worship”***. Al-Qurṭubī marks the change and calls it a deliberate turn, the way a man who has been describing a king to a friend stops when the king walks into the room and speaks to him directly. Al-Saʿdī reads the same shift as the answer to the praise: the servant has just said that God owns the day of account, and the only sensible reply to that sentence is to turn and address the owner himself.

Al-Baghawī opens his commentary on the sūrah with its names, and the first of them is the Opener of the Book. He notes that it is also called the Mother of the Qurʾān and the Seven Repeated Verses. Its seven lines are recited in every cycle of every prayer, which is why the community says this sentence more often than any other sentence on earth. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān divides the sūrah at this point: the earlier lines are praise offered to God, and the lines from here to the end are requests offered by the servant.

The report that Ibn Kathīr records from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim gives the turn a name. The Prophet ﷺ said that God has split the prayer into two halves, one for Him and one for His servant, and that when the worshipper reaches this sentence God answers that it is shared between the two, and that the servant will be given what he asks for. Ibn Kathīr places that report at the head of his reading of this verse, and al-Baghawī quotes it in the same place, so the early books treat the line as a moment of dialogue rather than a formula.

Al-Jalālayn keeps the reading short: the servant reserves worship for God alone and asks His help in that worship and in everything else. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a vow of obedience made to one Lord. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught his students that a person cannot say this sentence honestly while keeping a second loyalty in the corner of his heart, and that the plural in the words is a lesson of its own, because a lone man is taught to pray in the voice of a community. Al-Alūsī notes that the sūrah was placed at the head of the Book so that every reading of the Qurʾān begins with this pledge.

**WHY THE WORD FOR YOU COMES FIRST**

Al-Qurṭubī asks why the sentence puts the object before the verb, and answers with the habit of the Arabic language, which pushes the most important thing to the front. He tells the story of a man who insulted another and was ignored, until he called out that it was him he meant. The other replied that it was from him that he was turning away, and both of them put the weight first. Al-Saʿdī builds the whole meaning on that order: the placing means that worship is given to God and to nobody beside Him, and that help is sought from God and from nobody beside Him.

Ibn Kathīr gathers the same reading under two headings and says that the first half of the sentence clears the servant of associating partners with God, while the second clears him of trusting his own strength. He quotes the earliest scholars saying that the sūrah is the secret of the Qurʾān and that this sentence is the secret of the sūrah. The reason is plain once a reader sees the two halves of the sentence sitting together.

Al-Ṭabarī pauses over the word worship itself. In the speech of the Arabs, he says, the root carries the sense of lowering oneself and submitting, and a road is called muʿabbad when feet have worn it flat and travellers have tamed it. Worship in his reading is therefore not merely a set of movements but the entrusting of the self to its Lord. Al-Qurṭubī adds that the word also carries obedience, so that the servant who says it has handed over both his limbs and his will.

Al-Saʿdī widens that definition once more and calls the word a gathering name for everything God loves and accepts, whether it is done by the heart, the tongue or the body. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence as a promise to single out God alone, to obey Him, and to fear Him. A slave who is told that his master owns the day of account has only two options when the master is named. The sūrah moves the reader to the first of them before he has time to consider the second.

**WORSHIP WITHOUT HELP IS A BURDEN**

The sentence's second half is ***“and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help”***. Al-Qurṭubī reads the request as the search for help, support and success, and al-Saʿdī defines it as leaning on God for what brings benefit and turns away harm, with trust that He will deliver it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a request for help in worshipping God and for confidence in obeying Him, which is a small sentence doing a large amount of work.

Al-Ṭabarī explains why a person who has just promised to worship still needs to beg for help. He notes that the servant has admitted the duty in one breath and admitted his own weakness in the next, and that this is the honest position of a created being before his Maker. Al-Qurṭubī reports the observation that whoever accepts both halves of this verse has walked out of fatalism, which says that a person has no choice, and out of self-sufficiency, which says that a person needs nobody. The two errors sit on either side of the road, and the line passes between them.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn explains the words Muslims repeat during the call to prayer, that there is no power and no strength except with God, as a statement of this same reliance. The servant is declaring that he has no strength of his own to reach anything good. Al-Jalālayn says that the help asked for covers worship and everything else a person needs. A reader begins to see why the sūrah offers only these two requests before it asks for guidance in the next line.

The picture is a man with a heavy load and a wall he must climb. He can carry the load on his own back for a while, but the wall will stop him, and he needs a hand from above rather than advice from the ground. Ibn Kathīr's two headings meet here: a heart emptied of rival loyalties is only the first step, and a hand that has given up its own strength is the second. The verse is spoken in the voice of a community so that no one imagines he is climbing alone.
verses.6:
> Guide us along the Straight Path

**A REQUEST THAT NEVER GROWS OLD**

The sūrah has praised, and now it asks: ***“Guide us along the Straight Path”***. A reader might wonder why a person who already believes needs to ask for guidance at all, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān puts that question at the front of its reading of this verse before answering it. Its answer is that guidance is not a certificate that a person collects once. It is a road he walks, and the road must be walked again every morning.

Al-Qurṭubī reports the same understanding from the early scholars in a short and memorable sentence, that a man may be shown the road and then be cut off on it. That is why the request is for the guidance to continue rather than for it to begin. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a request to be inspired with the road that leads safely, and al-Ṭabarī says the word here means success granted by God, the same success that the previous line asked for in different words.

Al-Saʿdī sees two gifts folded into one request. The first is to be guided towards the road, which he explains as holding to the religion of Islam and leaving the religions beside it. The second is to be guided along the road, which covers every detail of belief and practice a person meets once he is on it. A reader who thinks he has finished with guidance does not know how many small decisions a single day asks of him.

The straightness of the road is the last thing the verse names. The Book describes it as a direction rather than a place: (42:52 — **“We have made it a light, by which We guide whoever We will of Our servants. And you are truly leading ˹all˺ to the Straight Path”**). Al-Jalālayn reads the request as help for the worshipper in his worship and in the rest of his affairs, and Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that the words are repeated in every unit of prayer because the need behind them never ends. Imagine a driver who reaches a familiar road and switches off his attention, and then meets a new junction in the dark.

**TWO ROADS THE BOOK HAS NAMED**

Ibn Kathīr collects the ways the Book uses the word guidance and shows that it covers both showing and enabling. He cites the verse that says God showed a human being his two options: (90:10 — **“shown them the two ways ˹of right and wrong”**), and he explains it as the explanation of the good road and the bad one. The request of this verse is therefore not for information, since the information has already been sent, but for the power to take the road a person has been shown.

Al-Baghawī notes that this line, like the rest of the sūrah, returns in every cycle of the prayer, so a worshipper repeats his plea for the road dozens of times a day without tiring of it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the request as a plea for the road of the prophets. Al-Alūsī records the old discussion about whether the sūrah was revealed at Makkah or Madīnah and notes that the difference does not touch the sense of this line, because both places needed the same request.

The early books are careful about one thing here. The request is not for a private road or a personal route, but for the road, the one that has already been marked by the people God blessed. Al-Saʿdī warns that a person who asks for guidance while refusing the company on that road has asked for something he does not want. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes that the sūrah places the request after the pledge of worship so that no reader mistakes the road for a project of his own design.

The image the scholars use is a mountain pass. The path is narrow, the drop on one side is real, and the travellers who walked it before have left marks a newcomer can follow. A driver who invents his own line across the mountain is not being brave, he is being careless with his own life. Al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence plain: the servant asks for help with his worship and with everything else, and the road is the answer to both.

**WHAT THE STRAIGHT ROAD MEANS IN A WEEK**

Al-Saʿdī defines the straight road as knowledge of the truth joined to action upon it, and the definition is worth carrying into ordinary days. A man may know that a loan taken on interest will do him harm and still sign the paper, and a man may act generously for years without ever asking whether his giving was placed where it belonged. The verse asks for a life in which knowing and doing stay joined.

The request also trains the worshipper to ask for small things. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sūrah has already asked for help in general terms and now asks for the one thing on which every other request depends. Ibn Kathīr's citations make the same point from the other side, since the Book describes guidance as a light that shows a person which step to take rather than as a map of the whole journey.

Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that a believer should ask for guidance before a decision, before a conversation and before a purchase, because the road is not a single event in a person's history. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that even prophets prayed this prayer, which removes any shame from an educated person who still asks. The most learned reader in the room is the one most in need of the request, since his mistakes have further to travel.

The sūrah is nearly finished, and it has asked for exactly one thing: not wealth, not long life and not victory, but a road. The next line explains whose road it is, and in doing so it draws the last and sharpest line in the chapter, because it tells the reader which company he is asking to travel with. Al-Baghawī's name for the sūrah fits the movement: seven lines recited in every prayer, a whole religion rehearsed in a single breath.
verses.7:
> the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray

**THE ROAD HAS A COMPANY**

The last line of the sūrah turns the request into a description: ***“the Path of those You have blessed”***. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the straight road needed a definition, because every road that leads to God is in some sense straight, and the verse supplies the definition by naming the travellers. He lists them from the Book itself as the angels, the prophets, the truthful, the witnesses and the righteous. He cites the verse that gathers the same company: (4:69 — **“will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous”**).

Ibn Kathīr reads the same list into the line and notes that the blessing named here is guidance itself, which is the greatest thing a servant can be given. Al-Saʿdī divides the company into the prophets who received the message, the truthful who carried it, the witnesses who gave their lives for it and the righteous whose conduct held it up in ordinary streets. A reader is being invited to measure his direction by the company he is keeping rather than by the confidence he feels.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read the blessed ones as the followers of Moses in the years when the blessing was still with them, the cloud that shaded them and the food that arrived without labour, before the community lost what it had been given. The report is a reminder inside a reminder for the reader: a road is not blessed because a community once walked it, but because the community keeps walking it. Al-Jalālayn notes that the verse names the company before it names the two groups who left it, and that the order matters because a reader needs a picture of the destination before he is warned about the ditches.

Imagine a first-year student arriving at a large campus. The buildings look the same, the paths run in several directions, and the only reliable guide is the line of seniors walking to the lecture hall. The verse is that line, drawn into a prayer, and the reader who has been asking for a road is now told that the road has footprints in it.

**THE TWO WAYS A TRAVELLER CAN LOSE THE ROAD**

The line then names what the reader is asking to be spared: ***“not those You are displeased with”***, and after it, ***“or those who are astray”***. The two failures are different, and the difference is the lesson of the verse. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the first as the fault of a person who knows the command of God and crosses it anyway, out of calculated stubbornness or in the service of a desire. It explains the second as the fault of a person who leaves the command behind out of ignorance and without thinking.

Al-Ṭabarī records the report of ʿAdī b. Ḥātim, who asked the Prophet ﷺ about this line and was told that the ones under displeasure are the Jews and the ones who went astray are the Christians. Ibn Kathīr records the same report and notes that the collection of al-Tirmidhī also carries it, with the comment that its chain is acceptable. Both books treat the answer as an identification of the two mistakes rather than as a license to insult a people. Ibn Kathīr supports it from the Book by pointing to the community that earned condemnation and the community that (5:77 — **“They misled many and strayed from the Right Way”**).

Al-Qurṭubī collects the readings that soften the identification, including the view that the verse describes two moral states that any community can fall into. He notes that the description fits a Muslim who knows better and refuses as surely as it fits anyone else. Al-Jalālayn draws out the grammar of the line and observes that placing the description in this position tells the reader that the blessed company is neither of those two groups. Al-Baghawī closes his commentary on the sūrah with the words that the congregation says at the end of it, asking God to accept the request.

The image is a map left on a table in a house with three travellers. One of them reads the map and walks the route. The second reads it, folds it up and takes a different road because the other road is shorter. The third never opens it and walks out of the door in the direction he happens to face. The verse asks to be among the first, and it names the other two so that no reader drifts into them without noticing.

**WHAT THIS LINE ASKS OF THE READER**

Al-Saʿdī draws a practical warning from the pairing of the two failures. A believer who has learned something of the religion should fear the first mistake more than the second, because knowledge raises the price of disobedience. A believer who has grown up in a Muslim household without ever learning the religion should fear the second, because a person can be lost on a familiar road. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that the correct response to both groups is neither mockery nor imitation, but a renewed request for guidance.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the line as a request for protection from both diseases, and al-Alūsī notes that the sūrah ends with this plea rather than with praise, which keeps a reader from finishing the chapter pleased with himself. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān records the practice of the Prophet ﷺ and the early community of pausing after this line, and it explains the pause as the place where the worshipper waits for the answer he has asked for.

Ibn Kathīr returns to the two traditions about the names of God that run through the chapter and notes that the sūrah closes in the same balance in which it opened: mercy has been named twice, the day of account has been named once. The chapter ends with a request for safety rather than a claim of achievement. Al-Qurṭubī's reading of the sūrah as a whole lands here, since a servant who has admitted that he depends on help cannot finish the prayer proud of himself.

Imagine a passenger who has been travelling with a guide for years and then decides he knows the route well enough to stop asking for directions. The sūrah was built for that passenger, and it puts the request for the road in his mouth at the end rather than at the beginning, after the praise, after the mercy and after the pledge. Ibn ʿUthaymīn taught that a person who says this last line honestly will find his day rearranged, because a traveller who has just asked for the road will not walk past a turning without looking.
